tldr: This paper presents RoboSynChallenge, a novel benchmark competition that trains bimanual robotic manipulation policies on large-scale synthetic simulation data and evaluates their generalization directly in unseen real-world environments. It demonstrates that models trained entirely on synthetic data can match or even outperform models trained on real-world data in physical manipulation tests.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of RoboSynChallenge. It illustrates the workflow: policies are trained using a combination of large-scale automatically synthesized data from simulation and a small amount of teleoperated real-world data, and then deployed to unseen real environments to evaluate their generalization performance.
overview:
Achieving generalization—enabling robots to flexibly adapt to unseen environments and objects—is one of the central goals in embodied AI. However, real-world data collection is expensive and time-consuming, resulting in limited data scale and narrow diversity. Conversely, simulation allows for the automatic generation of massive amounts of data, but the divergence in physics and visual appearance, known as the Sim2Real gap, poses a significant obstacle.

To address this, the authors launched RoboSynChallenge, a competition that uses a standardized benchmark to evaluate how effectively synthesized simulation data can be transferred to real-world dexterous manipulation. The defining feature of this competition is that participants can leverage an automated simulation data generator to produce and train on diverse action trajectories at scale, while final assessments are conducted exclusively in completely unseen real-world manipulation environments with varied backgrounds, lighting conditions, and distractor objects.

To establish benchmarks, the authors implemented baselines including modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs), running experiments on physical AgileX Piper bimanual setups. The results demonstrated that models trained solely on simulation data achieved success rates comparable to, and in some tasks even exceeding, those of models trained on real-world data. This benchmark establishes that high-quality synthetic data is a powerful asset for real-world robotic adaptation.
contributions: Constructed the first-of-its-kind Sim2Real transferability benchmark competition that couples large-scale automated simulation data generation with standardized physical robotic evaluation.

Established nine diverse bimanual manipulation tasks ranging from beginner to advanced difficulty, along with a rigorous real-world evaluation protocol that systematically perturbs backgrounds, lighting, and distractor objects.
Provided fully reproducible, open-source baseline implementations and experimental results covering Transformers, Diffusion Policy, modern VLA models (π₀, π₀.₅), and a World Action Model (Motus).

sections.heading: Inside the competition: Turning synthetic simulation data into real-world dexterity
sections.summary: This section comprehensively covers the objectives, novelty, data collection protocols, target tasks, evaluation metrics, and baseline models of RoboSynChallenge. Unlike traditional benchmarks relying on static, hand-collected datasets, it establishes a framework that leverages an automated synthetic data pipeline to evaluate policy generalization to unseen real environments.
sections.details:
This section details the vision and design behind RoboSynChallenge.

As background, end-to-end action learning has advanced rapidly through Transformers, diffusion models, and VLAs. However, existing benchmarks remain biased toward in-simulation testing (Sim2Sim) or static real-world datasets (Real2Real), lacking a unified framework to systematically measure Sim2Real transferability.

### 1.1 Novelty
RoboSynChallenge introduces three core innovations. The first is rigorous benchmarking of Sim2Real transfer. It assesses not just raw task success rates, but also robustness against real-world noise and domain shifts. The second is generative data streaming. Instead of distributing static datasets, it offers an extensible framework to procedurally generate infinite variations of environments and trajectories. The third is official evaluation on physical hardware. Submitted policies are strictly tested on physical bimanual robotic setups configured identically to the simulation environment.

### 1.2 Data
Data generation utilizes EmbodiChain, a GPU-accelerated simulation framework. It synthesizes large-scale trajectories containing RGB-D images, proprioception (joint angles and states), and contact events. For each task, 1,000 simulated episodes are generated with randomized lighting, materials, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics. In addition, to calibrate Sim2Real difficulty, a small teleoperated real-world dataset (60 trajectories per task across varying backgrounds and illumination) is provided.

### 1.3 Tasks and application scenarios
The physical evaluation platform consists of a dual-arm system using two 6-DoF AgileX Piper arms. Tasks are categorized into three difficulty tiers:
- Beginner tasks: Table tidying, bell ringing, water pouring, and basket carrying. These are short-horizon contact tasks with clear affordances.
- Intermediate tasks: Object handovers, drawer opening and storing, and operating a mixer. These involve coordinated bimanual motion, adaptive force control, and multi-object spatial relationships.
- Advanced tasks: Component assembly, pipetting, and sample filling. These require high geometric precision and multi-step sequential reasoning.

### 1.4–1.6 Evaluation metrics and baselines
Physical testing systematically perturbs individual factors—background textures (3 types), illumination conditions (3 types), unseen object instances, distractors (up to 8 non-target items), and spatial grid placement offsets—to compute the success rate (SR). Inference latency and action step counts are also recorded. Baseline implementations include five representative paradigms: ACT, Diffusion Policy, π₀, π₀.₅, and Motus, providing an open-source setup accessible to newcomers.

The major takeaway is that policies trained exclusively on simulation data rivaled or exceeded the performance of policies trained on real data.
sections.details:
The appendix details the EmbodiChain data generation framework and reports preliminary physical validation results for baseline policies.

### The three pillars of EmbodiChain
The reason simulation data transfers so effectively to hardware lies in EmbodiChain's design:
- 1. Generative simulation of training environments: Generative models construct simulation assets and optimize physical plausibility, while gradient-based placement optimization automatically generates reachable scenes for the dual-arm workspace.
- 2. Data scaling through domain augmentation: Trajectories are sampled to guarantee kinematic feasibility while maximizing diversity in task space. It also integrates a closed-loop error recovery module that detects slips or grasp failures, replanning and relabeling recovery actions.
- 3. Online Data Streaming (ODS): Dynamically varies textures, lighting, and sensor parameters at runtime, feeding data directly to the training loop via lock-free shared-memory circular buffers.

### Baseline evaluation results (Appendix B)
Remarkably, when VLAs (π₀, π₀.₅) and WAMs (Motus) trained purely on simulation data were deployed to physical hardware, they achieved success rates closely matching those of models trained on real data. In several scenarios, the simulation-trained models even outperformed their real-data-trained counterparts.

Because real-world data collection is laborious, it often suffers from narrow coverage. In contrast, the vast diversity and comprehensive coverage of error recovery trajectories in simulation contributed directly to strong real-world generalization. Furthermore, to ensure fair and timely competition execution, multiple identical backup physical testbeds were constructed in parallel.

captions.F4: Backup hardware environments constructed to support scalable and rapid real-world evaluation. Multiple identical setups replicate the exact robot positioning, cabling, and camera placements of the primary evaluation station.

takeaways: Diverse simulation data from automated synthetic pipelines (EmbodiChain) can serve as a powerful training resource, achieving real-world generalization on par with or superior to real robot data.
Successful Sim2Real transfer relies not just on visual fidelity, but heavily on functional diversity, including multi-directional approach sampling and comprehensive error-recovery motions.
Systematically perturbing backgrounds, lighting, distractor counts, and object positions during physical evaluation provides a practical, standardized benchmark for assessing policy robustness.
limitations: Because final scoring takes place on physical robots, organizers must manually run and score submitted policies in real environments, imposing limits on scalability and evaluation throughput.
The arms and cameras are fixed to a single specification (AgileX Piper) in both simulation and the real world, leaving cross-embodiment generalization across differing hardware morphologies untested.
